newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese troops arrive to garrison Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Chinese troops arrive to garrison Hong Kong.

text.p: Thousands of Chinese troops made a triumphal entry into Hong Kong at dawn on Tuesday to garrison China's new special region within hours of its return by Britain.

As all-night revellers still toasted the historic handover at midnight on Monday, the main body of China's garrison in the Special Administrative Region (SAR) swept across the border at three main points.

In armoured cars and trucks, they were welcomed by hundreds of Hong Kongers who turned out in driving rain with garlands, flowers and banners. Dragon dancers pranced along the route as lines of vehicles trundled by, soldiers standing erect and impassive in the wet.
A flotilla of warships steamed down the coastline to dock at Stonecutters Island on the northwestern edge of Hong Kong harbour. Helicopters were delayed by bad weather.

Although the blunt display of military force has drawn condemnation from Britain and milder rebuke from the United States, Beijing views it as a joyous affirmation of sovereignty after 156 years of colonial shame.
Pro-democracy activists regard the arrival of People's Liberation Army forces, and particularly armoured cars, as a provocative reminder of the 1989 Tiananmen massacre in Beijing.

Lined up neatly on the back of trucks, and clapping in unison, troops were sent off by banners and balloons on the mainland side of the border. Crowds stood 20-deep under umbrellas to watch the cavalcade.

In a midnight ceremony, heir to the British throne Prince Charles handed Hong Kong, its 6.4 million people and its trading bounty to China's President Jiang Zemin, leaving the Pearl of the Orient to a communist giant.

Charles and departing Governor Chris Patten, with his wife and their three daughters, were given a tearful farewell at Victoria Harbour aboard the royal yacht Britannia after a evening of imperial pomp and pageantry.

While party-goers cruised the clubs of Lan Kwai Fong, and young executives of Jardine Matheson -- the "Princely Hong" -- downed champagne at the company's penthouse, thousands of protesters took to the streets.
"In the eyes of the world, we call on the Chinese government to allow free, fair and democratic elections immediately," said leading democracy campaigner Martin Lee.
He was speaking to thousands of supporters at the building of the old elected legislature, dissolved by Beijing when Hong Kong was handed over and replaced by a China-picked assembly.

"The message is that we want democracy and we want it now," said activist Emily Lau at a rally in Statue Square. She led hundreds of people around the legislature, wrapping the building with a giant yellow ribbon.
"The yellow ribbon is our wish that democracy returns," said Lee Cheuk-yan, another prominent campaigner.
Other protesters carried banners reading "Down with Li Peng" and "Remember the June 4 slaughter", a reference to the 1989 killings that sparked fear and revulsion in Hong Kong.

The new legislature quickly met to pass an omnibus bill activating laws it adopted ahead of the formal handover. Its swearing-in was boycotted by British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
The bill approved a string of laws, including controversial curbs on political protests and the funding of political parties.

Post-handover chief executive Tung Chee-hwa, his administration and the provisional legislature were sworn in at a ceremony at the Hong Kong convention centre watched by 4,000 dignitaries from around the world.
The Shanghai-born shipping tycoon has made clear there will be limits to freedom and insults against Chinese leaders may not be tolerated.
Beijing has pledged that the region may keep its freewheeling capitalist lifestyle for a further 50 years under a "one country, two systems" formula negotiated with Britain.
To the strains of God Save the Queen, the Union Jack was lowered on the last major possession of the British empire at the stroke of midnight.
In its place rose the red five-star flag of the People's Republic of China and the bauhinia flower standard of the new SAR.
Patten, the 28th and last governor, who preferred a business suit to the plumed hat and ceremonial sword of office, bowed out with a terse telegram to the London Foreign Office.
"I have relinquished the administration of this Government. God Save the Queen," read his despatch, signed simply "Patten".
"We shall not forget you," Charles declared to the people of Hong Kong moments before he returned the capitalist powerhouse to Jiang, a Soviet-trained engineer.

Jiang said: "July 1, 1997 will go down in the annals of history as a day that merits eternal memory." From now on, he proclaimed, "Hong Kong compatriots have become true masters of this Chinese land".

With Charles at his side, Patten -- whose crusade for democracy in the twilight of colonial rule earned him Beijing's abiding hatred as a "whore" and "villain" -- showered kisses on well-wishers at the dockside.
Tung, a billionaire whose Chinese name means "build China", has promised popular elections for a new legislature next May.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said he expected China would be obliged to allow some dissent.
"The agreement says that there will be one China and two systems. And it's hard to have a system with free elections and freedom of speech and open press without dissent.
"I can't imagine how you could have it any other way."
Under a tropical downpour at sunset, Britain bade farewell to Hong Kong. A last exuberant hurrah featured bagpipers, opera divas, dragon dancers and massed choirs.

A crowd of 10,000 huddled under umbrellas while more than 100 million television viewers around the world witnessed the pomp and pageantry of Britain's retreat from a territory seized from the Celestial Kingdom in 19th century Opium Wars.
